beats.say: Welcome to Computer Vision.
In this first module, you'll learn what computer vision is, what makes an image digital, and how a vision system turns pixels into decisions.
Two close cousins. Computer vision, and digital image processing.
Image processing takes an image in and gives an image back. Computer vision takes an image in and gives understanding back.
Removing noise or sharpening is processing. Saying there are three people and a car is vision.
Image processing is cleaning your glasses. Computer vision is recognising your friend across the street.

scenes.title: A picture is a grid of numbers

beats.say: Here's a tiny five by five piece of a grayscale picture: a bright spot on a dark background.
An image is a function, f of x and y. At each position there is one brightness value, called the intensity.
beats.sql: f(x, y) = intensity at column x, row y

beats.say: Each cell is a pixel: a location, plus a value. The top left pixel, f of zero and zero, is twenty one, nearly black.
The centre pixel, f of two and two, is two hundred and fifty five: pure white.
Bright areas have high numbers. These nine middle pixels are all a hundred and eighty or more.
The edge pixels are in the low twenties, so they look dark. This grid of numbers is all the computer really has.

scenes.title: One number, three numbers, or just 0 and 1

beats.say: Pixels come in three common types. Let's describe that white centre pixel in each one.
Grayscale uses one number, from zero for black to two hundred and fifty five for white. Our centre pixel is two hundred and fifty five.
Colour uses three numbers: red, green and blue. White is full red, full green and full blue.
Binary keeps only zero or one, black or white. The bright centre becomes a one.
A vision system works in five stages.
First, acquisition. A camera or sensor captures the scene and turns it into numbers.
Preprocessing cleans the image: it removes noise, fixes brightness and contrast, and resizes.
Feature extraction finds useful patterns, like edges, corners, textures and shapes.
Recognition compares those features with learned patterns, to identify objects.
And decision making acts on the result: count, alert, steer, or diagnose.
Textbooks add stages like restoration, compression and segmentation. Later modules cover most of them.

scenes.title: Images come from the whole spectrum
rows: Imaging through clouds and at night

beats.say: Images aren't only photos. They can be made with any part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Gamma rays are used in nuclear medicine and astronomy.
X rays pass through soft material, so they're used for medical scans, airport baggage, and circuit boards.
Ultraviolet helps in microscopy and industrial inspection.
Visible and infrared light give us everyday cameras, satellites and night vision.
Radar uses microwaves to see through clouds and at night.
Put together, computer vision reads scans, drives cars, inspects factories, monitors crops, and analyses forensic video.

scenes.title: Which task is computer vision rather than image processing?
options: Counting people in a CCTV frame
scenes.good: That's right. Counting needs understanding of the content. The others output another image.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Counting needs understanding of the content. The others output another image.

beats.say: Quick check.

Tap your answer.

scenes.title: You're done when
items: An image is a grid of pixels

beats.say: That's Module 1.
You're done when:

and know images come from many kinds of radiation, not just visible light.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 2.
Here you'll see how the eye and the camera form an image, how light and surfaces combine, and how a continuous scene becomes a grid of numbers.

scenes.title: The human eye as a camera

beats.say: Light from the scene enters the eye through the cornea and the pupil.
The lens focuses it. It gets thicker for near objects, and thinner for far ones.
The focused image lands on the retina, at the back of the eye.
Cones, about six to seven million, work in bright light and see colour and fine detail. They cluster in the fovea.
Rods, about seventy five to a hundred and fifty million, work in dim light and see only shades of grey.
A camera does the same job: a lens focuses light onto a sensor of millions of cells, and each cell becomes a pixel.
The light a camera records depends on two things.
beats.sql: f(x, y) = i(x, y) × r(x, y)

beats.say: Illumination, i, is how much light falls on the scene. Reflectance, r, is the fraction the surface bounces back, from zero to one.
White paper reflects nine tenths of the light. In bright light, i is a thousand, so f is nine hundred.
Same paper, dim room. i drops to fifty, and f drops to forty five.
The paper didn't change. The illumination did. That's why vision systems must cope with lighting changes.
Black velvet has reflectance zero. However bright the light, it records zero.

scenes.title: Too few samples: blocky and jagged

beats.say: Here's one row of eight pixels: dark, then bright from position three, then dark again at the end.
Sampling decides how many points we measure. Let's keep only every second pixel.
Now the row is just four numbers: ten, ten, two hundred, two hundred.
To show it at full size again, nearest neighbour copies each sample twice.
Two pixels are now wrong. The edge has moved one step right, and the last dark pixel is gone.
Bilinear interpolation estimates the gap instead: halfway between ten and two hundred is a hundred and five. Smoother, but the lost detail stays lost.
Quantization decides how many values each pixel can take. Here's a smooth ramp of ten 8 bit values, rising by four each time.
Cut it to 3 bits, and there are only eight levels, each thirty two values wide.
The first seven values all fall into level three. The last three fall into level four.
Shown again as brightness, the smooth ramp becomes two flat bands, ninety six and a hundred and twenty eight.
That sudden jump between bands is false contouring: visible stripes in an area that should be smooth.
More levels cost more storage: width times height times bits. A thousand and twenty four square image at 8 bits is about eight point four million bits, one megabyte.

scenes.title: Who counts as a neighbour of p?

beats.say: Many operations look at a pixel's neighbours. Here's pixel p, in the middle.
The four neighbours, N four, are up, down, left and right. They form a cross.
The diagonal neighbours, N D, are the four corners.
All eight together are N eight.
Two pixels are adjacent if they're neighbours and both have values in a chosen set, say both white. Chains of adjacent pixels make paths, regions and boundaries.

scenes.title: Three ways to measure from (0, 0) to (3, 4)

beats.say: How far is pixel zero zero from pixel three four? It depends on how you're allowed to move.
Euclidean distance is the straight line: the square root of nine plus sixteen, which is five.
City block distance only moves along rows and columns, like the four neighbours: three plus four is seven.
Chessboard distance allows diagonal steps, like the eight neighbours, so it's the larger of the two: four.

scenes.title: An 8-bit image is reduced to 3 bits. How many grey levels remain?
scenes.good: That's right. Two to the power three is eight.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Two to the power three is eight.

beats.say: Quick check.
An eight bit image is reduced to three bits. How many grey levels remain?
Tap your answer.

scenes.title: You're done when
items: How the eye forms an image

beats.say: That's Module 2.
You're done when:
you can describe how the eye forms an image, with cones for colour and rods for dim light,
use f equals illumination times reflectance,
explain sampling and quantization and their artefacts,
and describe neighbours, adjacency and distance.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 3.
Now you'll look at how an image is stored: as a matrix of numbers, with properties like resolution, bit depth and channels.

scenes.title: A 3 × 3 grayscale image is a 3 × 3 matrix

beats.say: Here's a tiny grayscale image. It has three rows and three columns, so it's a three by three matrix.
By convention, the origin, zero zero, is the top left corner. Its value is twelve, almost black.
Rows count downwards, so y grows down the image. Row one, column two holds two hundred and twenty.
The brightest pixel is at row two, column two: two hundred and fifty five.
The left column is dark and the right column is bright, so this picture fades from black to white, left to right.

scenes.title: The same matrix in Python
scenes.code:
import numpy as np

img = np.array([[12, 40, 200],
                [15, 90, 220],
                [10, 60, 255]])
print(img.shape)
print(img[1, 2])

color = np.zeros((480, 640, 3), np.uint8)
print(color.shape)

beats.say: In Python, that matrix is a NumPy array.
Its shape is three rows by three columns.
Indexing is row first, then column. Row one, column two is two hundred and twenty.
A colour image stacks three matrices, one per channel. Here's a blank one, 640 pixels wide and 480 tall.
Its shape is height, then width, then three channels.

scenes.title: Resolution, channels and bit depth add up fast

beats.say: Four properties describe an image. Let's take one full H D video frame.
Resolution is the number of pixels: nineteen twenty by ten eighty, about two point one million.
Aspect ratio is width divided by height. That's one point seven eight, the same as sixteen by nine.
Channels: one for grayscale, three for R G B, four when there's transparency.
Bit depth is bits per channel. Eight bits gives two hundred and fifty six levels. Medical images often use sixteen.
Multiply it out: two point one million pixels, times three bytes, is about six point two megabytes for one frame.
At thirty frames a second, that's about a hundred and eighty six megabytes every second. That's why video is compressed.

scenes.title: Why green looks brighter than blue

beats.say: In R G B, each pixel mixes red, green and blue light. All zeros is black, all two fifty fives is white.
To make gray, a plain average treats all three colours the same. Pure red, green and blue all get eighty five.
But our eyes are most sensitive to green, and least to blue. So the standard formula weights them.
Pure red becomes seventy six.
Pure green becomes a hundred and fifty: much brighter.
And pure blue only twenty nine. Same average, very different brightness. Try it in the lab in the course.
Going back, gray to colour, just copies the gray value into all three channels. The lost colour can't come back.
There are two ways to store a picture.
A raster image is a grid of pixels. A vector image describes shapes with maths, as lines and curves.
Photos and camera frames are raster. Logos and fonts are usually vector.
Enlarge a raster image and it gets blocky. A vector is redrawn from its shapes, so it stays sharp.
Computer vision almost always works on raster images. More pixels mean more detail, but more storage and computing.

scenes.title: The shape of a 640 × 480 RGB image array (height × width × channels) is…
scenes.good: That's right. Rows, which is the height, come first, then columns, then three channels.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Rows, which is the height, come first, then columns, then three channels.

beats.say: Quick check.
What is the shape of a six forty by four eighty R G B image array, written as height, width, channels?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 3.
You're done when:
you can describe an image as a matrix, and colour as three stacked matrices,
explain resolution, bit depth, channels and aspect ratio,
convert colour to grayscale with the weighted formula,
and tell raster from vector graphics.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 4.
Images are matrices, so linear algebra and signal processing carry straight over. Let's build the toolkit.
A scalar is one number. A vector is a list of numbers, like a feature vector describing one image. A matrix is a grid.
The dot product of two vectors multiplies matching entries, and adds them up.
One times four is four.
Two times five is ten.
Three times six is eighteen.
Add them: four plus ten plus eighteen is thirty two. The dot product measures how similarly two vectors point.

scenes.title: Dot products and matrices in code
scenes.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
print(a @ b)

A = np.array([[2, 0],
              [0, 1]])
p = np.array([3, 1])
print(A @ p)
print(np.linalg.det(A))

beats.say: Here are the same two vectors in NumPy.
The at sign computes the dot product. Thirty two, as before.
Now a two by two matrix A: two, zero, zero, one. And a point p at three, one.
A times p is two times three plus zero, and zero plus one times one. The point moves to six, one.
The determinant, a d minus b c, is two times one minus zero: two.

scenes.title: Every 2 × 2 matrix moves points by one rule

beats.say: Multiplying a point by a two by two matrix moves it. Every point moves by the same rule, so it's a linear transformation.
beats.sql: [a b; c d] · [x, y] = [ax + by, cx + dy]

beats.say: Watch what happens to the two unit arrows. The stretch matrix doubles x, and leaves y alone. Area doubles, so the determinant is two.
This one rotates by ninety degrees. Nothing grows, so the determinant is one.
The shear slides the top sideways, but keeps the area: determinant one.
A negative determinant means the plane is mirrored.
And a zero determinant squashes everything onto one line. Both arrows land on the same line, so there's no inverse.
For the stretch, the x direction is only stretched, never turned. That's an eigenvector, and its eigenvalue, the stretch factor, is two. Try the presets in the lab in the course.

scenes.title: Find the direction of greatest variance

beats.say: Here are ten images, each described by two features. They're clearly related: when one goes up, so does the other.
Principal component analysis first standardises the features. These two are already on the same scale.
Next it computes the covariance matrix: how the two features vary together. Here it's strongly positive.
Its top eigenvector is the first principal component. It runs right along the cloud.
Its eigenvalue, about eight hundred and seventy six, is the variance along that line. The second component has only about eighteen.
So the first component keeps ninety eight percent of the variance. Project each point onto the line, and two features become one.
The catch: the new feature is a mixture of the old ones, so it's harder to interpret.
An image is a two dimensional signal, so signal processing tools carry straight over.
The Fourier transform rewrites the image as a sum of waves. f f t shift moves the low frequencies to the centre.
Low frequencies are smooth areas. High frequencies are edges and fine detail.
A low pass filter keeps only the centre, the low frequencies. A high pass filter would keep the edges instead.
Multiplying in frequency is the same as convolving in space. That's what makes big filters fast.
The inverse transform turns the result back into pixels: a smoother image.
And the Fast Fourier Transform is quick: for a thousand and twenty four samples, about ten thousand steps instead of a million.

scenes.title: A matrix has determinant 0. What happens to shapes?
options: They collapse onto a line or point
scenes.good: That's right. Zero area scale means the transform squashes the plane.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Zero area scale means the transform squashes the plane.

beats.say: Quick check.
A matrix has determinant zero. What happens to shapes?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 4.
You're done when:
you can use vectors, matrices and the dot product,
read a two by two matrix as a transformation, with its determinant and eigenvectors,
explain how P C A keeps the directions of greatest variance,
and describe convolution, filtering and the Fourier transform.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 5.
Here you'll meet the Python libraries for computer vision, and learn which one to reach for.

scenes.title: Four libraries, four jobs
rows: Every image is a NumPy array

beats.say: Four libraries cover most computer vision work in Python. Pick by the job.
Open C V handles images and video: reading, resizing, filtering, finding edges, drawing boxes, reading a webcam.
NumPy does fast arrays and maths. Every image is a NumPy array underneath.
scikit learn is for classical machine learning: splitting data, classic models, and metrics.
PyTorch and TensorFlow are for deep learning: building and training C N Ns on G P Us.
So, to train a C N N, reach for PyTorch or TensorFlow, not scikit learn.

scenes.title: Load, inspect, convert, save
scenes.code:
import cv2

img = cv2.imread("street.jpg")   # NumPy array, (H, W, 3), uint8
print(img.shape)
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
small = cv2.resize(img, (224, 224))
cv2.imwrite("gray.jpg", gray)

print(gray.shape)
print(small.shape)

beats.say: Say street dot jpg is a photo 1280 pixels wide and 720 tall. imread loads it.
It comes back as a NumPy array: height, width, then three colour channels.
c v t Color converts it to grayscale, from B G R. One channel is left.
resize makes a two twenty four by two twenty four copy, a common input size for networks.
imwrite saves the gray version as gray dot jpg.
Print the shapes: gray has no channel axis, and small is two twenty four square, with three channels.
Take a sky blue pixel: red one thirty five, green two oh six, blue two thirty five.
Open C V stores the channels backwards: blue first, then green, then red.
So the array holds two thirty five, two oh six, one thirty five.
Matplotlib expects R G B. It reads the first number as red.
Lots of red, little blue. Your blue sky shows up orange.
The fix: convert first, with c v t Color, B G R to R G B.
PyTorch and TensorFlow both work with tensors: multi dimensional arrays that can live on a G P U.
In PyTorch you build a model, for example with n n dot Sequential. The forward pass runs a batch through it.
A loss, like cross entropy, scores how wrong the predictions are.
loss dot backward computes every gradient for you. That's automatic differentiation.
The optimiser, such as Adam, steps the weights a little downhill.
Then the loop repeats: forward, loss, backward, step.
TensorFlow's Keras wraps this up: stack layers, then compile and fit. It has strong tools for phones, browsers and servers.
For classical machine learning, scikit learn follows the same four steps. Say we have a thousand labelled images.
Train test split with test size zero point two keeps twenty percent aside: eight hundred to train, two hundred to test.
Fit trains the model on the eight hundred.
Predict labels the two hundred test images it has never seen.
Then evaluate. If a hundred and eighty predictions are right, accuracy is a hundred and eighty over two hundred: zero point nine.
Models need numbers, so categories must be encoded.
Label encoding gives each category one number: red zero, green one, blue two.
But that implies an order, as if green sits between red and blue. Fine for small, medium, large, and for targets.
One hot encoding gives each category its own column, with a single one.
Green is zero, one, zero. No false order, so it's the choice for unordered inputs.

scenes.title: Colours look wrong when you plot an OpenCV image with Matplotlib. Why?
scenes.good: That's right. Open C V uses B G R order. Convert with c v t Color, B G R to R G B.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Open C V uses B G R order. Convert with c v t Color, B G R to R G B.

beats.say: Quick check.
Colours look wrong when you plot an Open C V image with Matplotlib. Why?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 5.
You're done when:
you can choose the right library for a task,
load, inspect and convert an image with Open C V, remembering B G R,

and pick label encoding for order, one hot for unordered categories.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 6.
Now you'll enhance images: change each pixel's brightness with simple rules, read histograms, and pick the right colour space.

scenes.title: s = T(r): each pixel changes on its own

beats.say: A point operation changes each pixel using only its own value. r goes in, s comes out.
The negative flips it: two fifty five minus r. Two hundred becomes fifty five. Handy for white details in X rays.
The log transform brightens dark values strongly. Fifty jumps to a hundred and eighty one.
beats.sql: log: s = c·log(1 + r),  c = 255 / log 256

beats.say: Gamma below one also brightens. With gamma zero point four, a hundred becomes a hundred and seventy five.
Gamma above one darkens. With gamma two point five, a hundred drops to twenty five.
Thresholding makes a binary image: two fifty five if r is at least the threshold, otherwise zero.

scenes.title: Read the curve: above the line brightens

beats.say: Plotting T as a curve shows what a transform does at a glance.
The diagonal is no change: s equals r.
Here's gamma zero point four. Every point sits above the line, so every value gets brighter. Mid gray, a hundred and twenty eight, rises to about a hundred and ninety four.
And gamma two point five. Its points sit below the line, so it darkens. Mid gray falls to about forty five.
Both curves meet at black and white. Screens and cameras use this gamma correction. Try it in the lab in the course.

scenes.title: Spread out the crowded dark levels

beats.say: A histogram counts how many pixels have each grey level. Bunched left means dark, bunched right means bright, narrow means low contrast.
Here's the course example: eight levels, sixty four pixels. Half of them crowd into the three darkest levels.
Equalization uses the running total, the cumulative histogram, as the transform.
Level zero: eight pixels so far. Seven times eight over sixty four is about one.
Level one: twenty four so far, which maps to about three.
Level two: thirty two so far, which maps to four.
So zero, one and two become one, three and four. The crowded dark levels get pushed apart, and the brightest level always maps to seven.
CLAHE does this on small tiles, bringing out detail in both shadows and highlights.

scenes.title: Pick the space that separates what you care about

beats.say: Images can be stored in different colour spaces. Each separates different information.
R G B, or B G R in Open C V, is for display and storage.
Grayscale keeps brightness only: great for edges, shape, and speed.
H S V splits hue, the colour, from saturation and value, the brightness. Perfect for tracking a red ball.
LAB measures colour differences the way people see them.
And Y C r C b separates brightness from colour, for video compression and skin detection.

scenes.title: Same red ball, sun and shade

beats.say: Here's one red ball, in sunlight and in shade.
In B G R, every number changes. The red value halves, from two twenty to one ten.
In H S V, only value, the brightness, changes: two twenty to one ten.
Hue stays at zero, red, and saturation stays at two twenty. So a hue range finds the ball under any lighting.

scenes.title: A histogram squeezed into a narrow band means…
scenes.good: That's right. Few levels are used, so the image looks flat.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Few levels are used, so the image looks flat.

beats.say: Quick check.
A histogram squeezed into a narrow band means…
Tap your answer.
That's Module 6.

Welcome to Module 7.
Noise is unwanted random variation in pixel values. Here you'll learn to recognise it, and to remove it with spatial filters.

scenes.title: Know your noise
rows: Random pure white and black dots

beats.say: Noise is unwanted random variation in pixel values. There are four common kinds.
Gaussian noise is fine grain everywhere, from sensor electronics and heat.
Salt and pepper noise is random pure white and black dots, from faulty pixels or transmission errors.
Speckle is grain that scales with brightness, typical of ultrasound and radar.
And Poisson, or shot noise, is worse in dark images, where only a few photons are counted.

scenes.title: Slide a 3 × 3 mean kernel over the pixels

beats.say: Here's a five by five patch of a flat gray image, around twelve, with one salt dot of two fifty five in the middle.
A spatial filter uses a small window, a kernel. The mean kernel is three by three, every weight one ninth.
Centre it on row one, column one. Add the nine pixels under it: three hundred and forty five. Divide by nine: about thirty eight.
Slide one step right. This window adds to three hundred and forty eight, so about thirty nine.
Centred on the dot itself, the nine values add to three hundred and forty six: about thirty eight.
And so on to the last full window, at row three, column three: three forty seven, about thirty nine.
At the borders, we pad the image by copying edge pixels, adding zeros, or mirroring.

scenes.title: Mean spreads the dot; median removes it

beats.say: Here are all nine outputs from the middle of the patch.
With the mean filter, every window contains the dot, so every output is pulled up to thirty eight or thirty nine.
One bright pixel has become a three by three gray smudge. Mean is a linear filter: a weighted sum.
The median filter sorts each window and takes the middle value instead. Every output is eleven or twelve.
beats.sql: non-linear: output = middle of sorted window

beats.say: The dot is simply gone, and the patch is back to its flat gray.

scenes.title: Why the median ignores the dot

beats.say: Here are the nine values under the kernel when it's centred on the dot.
The mean adds them, three hundred and forty six, and divides by nine. About thirty eight. The dot drags it up.
The median sorts them first.
The two fifty five ends up at the far end, where it can't affect the middle.
The middle value, fifth of nine, is twelve. The dot vanishes.

scenes.title: Four filters on the same window

beats.say: Let's run four filters on that same window, centred on the dot. The clean value would be about twelve.
Mean gives thirty eight. It reduces Gaussian grain, but blurs edges.
Gaussian weights near neighbours more, so the centre counts four sixteenths. The dot pulls it to seventy two. It's a smoother, more natural blur for fine grain.
Median gives twelve. It's the right first choice for salt and pepper, and it keeps edges sharper.
Bilateral only averages neighbours that are both close and similar in brightness. Nothing is similar to the dot, so it stays two fifty five.
That's exactly how bilateral keeps edges: it smooths flat areas, but stops where brightness jumps. Try the filters in the lab in the course.

scenes.title: Bigger kernels: less noise, more blur

beats.say: We made a test image of wide gray stripes, added Gaussian noise, and measured P S N R against the clean image. Higher is better.
With no filter, the noisy image scores eighteen point eight decibels.
A three by three mean filter removes much of the grain: twenty three point four.
Bigger kernels remove more noise, but blur the stripe edges more. Five by five drops to twenty two, seven by seven to twenty point seven.
By eleven by eleven, the blur costs as much as the noise did: back to eighteen point eight. Pick the smallest kernel that removes enough noise.

scenes.title: Which filter is non-linear?
scenes.good: That's right. Sorting and picking the middle value isn't a weighted sum.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Sorting and picking the middle value isn't a weighted sum.

beats.say: Quick check.
Which filter is non-linear?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 7.
You're done when:
you can recognise Gaussian, salt and pepper, speckle and Poisson noise,
explain how a kernel slides over an image,
choose between mean, Gaussian, median and bilateral filters,
and describe the trade off between smoothing and sharp edges.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 8.
Geometric transformations change where pixels are, not their values.
You'll learn the common transforms, the matrix behind them, and why interpolation is needed.
Most geometric transforms fit in one matrix, two rows by three columns. The new x is a times x, plus b times y, plus t x. The new y works the same way with c, d and t y.
beats.sql:
x′ = a·x + b·y + tx
y′ = c·x + d·y + ty

beats.say: Translation keeps a and d at one, b and c at zero, and puts the shift in the last column, t x and t y.
Rotation by theta fills the left part with cos theta and sine theta, with a minus sign on b.
Scaling puts s x and s y on the diagonal.
Shear in x puts the shear amount in b, so x slides further the larger y gets.
Reflection puts minus one in a, which mirrors x around zero.
All five keep straight lines straight, and parallel lines parallel. That's what affine means. Cropping is the odd one out: it's just array slicing.

scenes.title: Move the corners of a square

beats.say: Here's a square, two pixels wide, with corners A, B, C and D. Let's push its corners through each matrix.
Shift by three and one: add three to every x and one to every y. Every corner moves the same way.
Rotate ninety degrees around the origin. Cos is zero and sine is one, so the new x is minus y, and the new y is x.
Corner C, at two, two, lands on minus two, two. The square turns a quarter turn.
Scale by two doubles every number, so the square becomes four pixels wide.
Shear by zero point five adds half of y to x. The bottom corners, where y is zero, stay put.
The top corners slide right by one. The square becomes a slanted shape, but its opposite sides are still parallel.
Picture two railway rails, at x minus ten and x ten, running away from the camera.
An affine shear slides both rails sideways as y grows, but the gap between them stays twenty, all the way.
A perspective transform uses a three by three matrix called a homography. Its extra row divides every point by w, which grows with distance.
beats.sql: homography:  x′ = x ÷ w,  y′ = y ÷ w,  w = 1 + 0.02·y

beats.say: At distance twenty, the gap shrinks to fourteen point three.
beats.sql: homography:  x′ = x ÷ w,  y′ = y ÷ w,  w = 1 + 0.02·y

beats.say: After a transform, an output pixel rarely lands exactly on an input pixel. This one maps back to x one point four, y zero point three.
It sits between four input pixels, with values fifty, ninety, thirty and seventy.
Nearest neighbour just copies the closest pixel, at one, zero. The answer is fifty. Fast, but blocky.
Bilinear blends all four. Each weight is how close the point is in x, times how close it is in y. For one, zero, that's zero point six times zero point seven: zero point four two.
Multiply and add: twenty one, plus twenty five point two, plus five point four, plus eight point four. Sixty. Smooth, and the usual default.
Bicubic blends the sixteen nearest pixels: smoothest, but slower.

An edge is where brightness changes quickly: the outline of an object, a shadow line, a texture boundary.
Since edges are about change, edge detectors are built from derivatives.

scenes.title: An edge is a big change

beats.say: Here's a row of six pixels: dark, dark, dark, then suddenly bright. The edge sits between ten and two hundred.
The first derivative is the change from each pixel to the next. Flat areas give zero, but at the edge it jumps to one ninety.
The second derivative, the change of that change, goes plus one ninety, then minus one ninety. It crosses zero exactly at the edge.
beats.note: second derivative: crosses zero at the edge

scenes.title: One step of the Sobel filter

beats.say: A three by three patch: dark on the left, bright on the right.
Sobel G x adds the right column, subtracts the left, and counts the middle row twice.
Top row: minus twenty, plus one eighty. One sixty.
Middle row, weighted two: minus fifty, plus three eighty. Three thirty.
Bottom row: minus twenty, plus one eighty five. One sixty five.
Add them up: G x is six fifty five. A huge response.
G y does the same top to bottom. The bottom row gives two sixty five, the top row two sixty. G y is just five.
So the gradient magnitude is about six fifty five, pointing almost exactly to the right. That's a vertical edge.
Prewitt drops the double weight, Scharr uses three, ten, three, and the Laplacian uses the second derivative.

scenes.title: Keep weak edges only if they touch strong ones

beats.say: Canny blurs, takes the Sobel gradient, and thins edges to one pixel wide. Here are gradient strengths along one thinned edge.
The last stage uses two thresholds. With Canny one hundred, two hundred, anything at two hundred or more is a strong edge.
Anything below one hundred is dropped straight away.
Between the two are weak edges: one fifty, one twenty, one thirty and one seventy.
Hysteresis keeps a weak pixel only if it connects to a strong one. One fifty and one twenty chain to two fifty; one seventy touches two ten.
One thirty is stranded, so it goes too. Isolated noise disappears; real edges stay connected.
Harris slides a small window and sums the squared Sobel gradients inside it.
Here are three tiny black and white patches. In a flat area, nothing changes, so R is zero.
On a vertical edge, there's lots of change in x, but none in y. The determinant is zero, so R goes negative: minus three six eight.
At a corner, both directions change. The determinant is two thousand four hundred and forty eight, and R is a big positive two thousand and fifteen.
Large R means corner: an easy landmark to find again for matching and tracking.
Here's a row of a binary image. There's a tiny white speck on the left, and a real object of five pixels.
Erosion keeps a pixel white only if the whole three pixel element fits inside white.
The speck vanishes, and the object shrinks by one pixel on each side.
Dilation then turns a pixel white if the element touches any white. The object grows back to five pixels, but the speck can't come back.
That's opening. Closing is the reverse, dilation then erosion, and it fills small holes instead.

scenes.title: Pick the threshold that splits best

beats.say: Morphology needs a binary image, and thresholding makes one. Here are ten pixel values.
Otsu tries a threshold and measures how separate the two groups are: the share in each group, times the squared gap between their means.
At one hundred, it's five against five, with means thirty six and one eighty. The score is five one eight four.
Otsu tries every level and keeps the largest. Here that's the five and five split. In Open C V, you just add the Otsu flag.

scenes.title: You want to remove small white specks but keep the main object's size. Which operation?
scenes.good: That's right. Opening erodes to remove the specks, then dilates to restore the object.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Opening erodes to remove the specks, then dilates to restore the object.

Welcome to Module 10.
To match the same object across two photos, taken from different angles, distances or lighting, we need features that stay recognisable.
We want to find the same object in two photos, taken from different angles, distances or lighting.
First, find keypoints: interesting, repeatable locations, like corners or blobs.
Then describe the patch around each one as a vector of numbers. That's the descriptor.
Do the same for the second photo.
Matching is just finding descriptors that are close together. A good descriptor is invariant: its numbers barely change when the image is scaled, rotated or brightened.

scenes.title: ORB matches by counting different bits

beats.say: ORB describes each keypoint with a binary string of brightness comparisons. Here's a short, eight bit query descriptor.
Hamming distance counts the bits that differ. Candidate A differs in just one place, bit six.
Candidate B is the exact opposite: all eight bits differ.
Candidate C differs in two bits, three and eight.
The smallest distance wins, so the query matches A. Real ORB strings have two hundred and fifty six bits, and counting bits is very fast.
SIFT finds blobs at every scale, gives each keypoint its dominant direction, then builds its descriptor.
Sixteen by sixteen pixels, split into four by four cells, each with an eight bin gradient histogram. That's one hundred and twenty eight numbers.
SURF approximates SIFT with box filters: several times faster, slightly less precise.
ORB is binary, matched with Hamming distance, the fastest, and free to use.
So: most reliable matches, choose SIFT. Real-time on limited hardware, choose ORB.
HOG describes a whole window by its edge directions. Each eight by eight cell gets a histogram with nine bins, from zero to one eighty degrees.
A pixel with direction ten degrees and magnitude five votes five into the first bin.
Eighty five degrees, magnitude twelve, lands in bin four, eighty to one hundred degrees.
Eighty eight with nine, and ninety five with six, land there too. Bin four reaches twenty seven.
One seventy degrees, magnitude three, goes in the last bin.
The tall bar says this cell is mostly gradients near ninety degrees: one strong edge running across it.
A person-sized window is sixty four by one hundred and twenty eight pixels.
Eight by eight cells give eight across and sixteen down.
Blocks are two by two cells, sliding one cell at a time. That's seven by fifteen: one hundred and five blocks.
Each block holds four cells of nine bins: thirty six numbers, normalised together so lighting matters less.
Join them all: one hundred and five times thirty six is three thousand seven hundred and eighty features, ready for an S V M.

scenes.title: Which descriptor is binary and matched with Hamming distance?
scenes.good: That's right. ORB uses rotated BRIEF, a bit string.
scenes.bad: Not quite. ORB uses rotated BRIEF, a bit string.

Machine learning lets computers learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
Machine learning comes in three kinds.
Supervised learning learns from labelled examples. Classification predicts a category, like cat or dog.
Regression predicts a number, like age or price.
Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels, like clusters.
And reinforcement learning has an agent learn by trial and error, from rewards.
Whatever the kind, the workflow is the same: collect data, preprocess, develop the model, then evaluate it on data it has never seen.
beats.sql: data collection → preprocessing → model development → evaluation

beats.say: Here are eight labelled training points: four in class A, four in class B.
A new point arrives at forty eight, forty five. Which class is it?
With k equals one, we copy the single closest point. That's a B, about fifteen point six away.
With k equals three, we add the next two: two A points, at sixteen point four and twenty three.
The vote is two A against one B, so the answer flips to A. The choice of k matters, and an odd k avoids ties.

scenes.title: Not too simple, not too complex

beats.say: Compare how a model scores on training data and on test data.
An underfit model is too simple. It's poor on both. That's high bias.
An overfit model memorises the training data, noise and all. Great on training, poor on test. That's high variance.
More complex models lower bias but raise variance. We want the balance in the middle.
To fix overfitting: more data, simpler models, data augmentation, or regularisation. Lasso can set weights exactly to zero; Ridge shrinks them all smoothly.
beats.sql: Lasso (L1): + |weights|     Ridge (L2): + weights²     Elastic Net: both

scenes.title: Every fold gets its turn as the test

beats.say: Cross-validation splits the data into k folds. Here, k is five.
Round one trains on folds two to five, and tests on fold one.
Round two rotates: fold two becomes the test.
Keep rotating until every fold has been tested exactly once.
Average the five scores for a fair estimate. Use this to tune settings like k or tree depth, with grid search or random search. Stratified folds keep class proportions the same.
A defect detector finds ninety of a hundred real defects, and raises sixty false alarms.
Ninety true positives, and ten misses: false negatives.
Sixty false positives: alarms on parts that were fine.
Precision asks: of the alarms, how many were right? Ninety out of one fifty. Zero point six.
Recall asks: of the real defects, how many did we find? Ninety out of a hundred. Zero point nine.
F1 combines them: two times zero point six times zero point nine, divided by one point five. Zero point seven two.
On imbalanced data, accuracy can hide those misses and false alarms. So use precision, recall, F1, and the area under the R O C curve.

scenes.good: That's right. A big gap between training and test performance means the model is memorising.

A neuron takes inputs, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function.
Stack neurons into layers, and many hidden layers make deep learning.
Here's one neuron. Each input is multiplied by its weight: one, minus one, and zero point six.
Add the bias, minus zero point one, and z is zero point five.
Then an activation adds non-linearity. ReLU keeps positives and zeroes negatives, so it outputs zero point five. For z of minus three, it would output zero.
Sigmoid squashes the same z into zero to one: about zero point six two. Tanh gives about zero point four six.
For many classes, softmax turns scores two, one and zero point one into probabilities that add up to one.

scenes.title: The learning rate decides the step

beats.say: Training runs forward, measures the loss, backpropagates, then nudges every weight against its gradient.
Take a toy loss, w squared, whose lowest point is at zero. Its gradient is two w. Start at w equals four.
beats.sql: Loss = w²   ·   gradient = 2w   ·   w ← w − η × 2w

beats.say: With a learning rate of zero point one, w crawls: three point two, two point five six, and so on. Painfully slow.
beats.sql: Loss = w²   ·   gradient = 2w   ·   w ← w − η × 2w

beats.say: With zero point four, it drops to zero point eight, then zero point one six. It reaches the minimum in a few steps.
beats.sql: Loss = w²   ·   gradient = 2w   ·   w ← w − η × 2w

beats.say: With one point one, every step overshoots: minus four point eight, then five point seven six, then further out. The loss grows. It diverges.
beats.sql: Loss = w²   ·   gradient = 2w   ·   w ← w − η × 2w

scenes.title: Follow an image through the layers

beats.say: A C N N starts with the image: thirty two by thirty two pixels, three colour channels.
A convolutional layer slides twelve learned three by three filters over it. With padding one, each feature map stays thirty two by thirty two.
ReLU is applied to every value. The size doesn't change.
Max pooling keeps the largest of every four values, halving width and height: sixteen by sixteen by twelve.
Flatten lines those up into one vector of three thousand and seventy two.
Fully connected layers combine the features, and softmax gives the final class probabilities.

scenes.title: How big is the feature map?

beats.say: One formula gives the output width: input width, minus kernel size, plus twice the padding, divided by the stride, plus one.
A five by five kernel with no padding on a thirty two wide input gives twenty eight. The map shrinks.
Add padding two, and it's thirty two again. That's called same size.
A three by three kernel with padding one also keeps thirty two. That's the convolution layer we just traced.
And two by two pooling with stride two fits the same formula: sixteen.
AlexNet won ImageNet in twenty twelve and started the deep learning boom. VGG stacked three by three convolutions very deep.
ResNet adds each layer's input to its output. Those skip connections let networks train with over a hundred layers. Inception runs several filter sizes side by side.
YOLO resizes the image, splits it into a seven by seven grid, and each cell predicts boxes and class scores. In version one, that's two boxes and twenty classes per cell.
So one forward pass outputs seven by seven by thirty numbers, and non-maximum suppression removes duplicate boxes.
Instead of training from scratch, start from a model already trained on a huge dataset like ImageNet.
Feature extraction freezes those layers, and trains only a new final layer for your classes.
Fine-tuning also adjusts some pre-trained layers, with a small learning rate.
Either way, you need far less data and time. It's the usual choice in practice.

Welcome to Module 13.
Object detection looks at one frame and says what's there and where.
Object tracking follows those objects across frames, and keeps a consistent identity for each.
Most trackers use tracking by detection. First, a detector like YOLO finds boxes in each frame.
Next, predict where each existing track should be now.
Then associate: decide which new detection belongs to which track.
Matched tracks are updated. Unmatched detections start new tracks, and tracks lost too long are retired.
The updated tracks feed the next prediction, and the loop repeats every frame.

scenes.title: Predict, then update, frame by frame

beats.say: A person moves right at ten pixels per frame. To keep it simple, the speed stays fixed, and each prediction adds one to the uncertainty.
Frame two. Predict: ninety plus ten is one hundred. Time has passed, so uncertainty grows from three to four.
The detector says one hundred and ten, with uncertainty one. The gain is four divided by four plus one: zero point eight.
New estimate: one hundred, plus zero point eight times ten. One hundred and eight, closer to the more trusted detection. Uncertainty shrinks to zero point eight.
Frame three, the person is hidden. No detection, so the prediction, one eighteen, becomes the estimate, and uncertainty keeps growing.
Frame four, they're back at one twenty five. The prediction was shakier, so the gain rises to about zero point seven four, and the estimate lands near one twenty five point eight.
Prediction alone drifts, and measurements alone jitter and vanish. Together, they're smooth and robust.
Three tracks, three detections. Each cell is a cost: how unlikely that pairing is, from distance, box overlap, or appearance.
A greedy matcher grabs the cheapest pair first: track one with detection one, cost one.
Next cheapest that's still free: track three with detection three, cost four.
That forces track two onto detection two, cost nine. Total: fourteen.
The Hungarian algorithm checks the whole assignment. Track one takes D two, track two takes D one, track three takes D three. Total: eight.
It always returns the cheapest answer, even when it's wrong. If two similar people stand close, their costs are nearly equal, and a small change can swap their I Ds.
Someone walks behind a pillar for five seconds. The detector sees nothing, but the track is kept in a lost state, not deleted.
The Kalman filter keeps predicting their path, with growing uncertainty.
When a new detection appears, gating checks it's in a plausible place.
A re-identification network compares its appearance embedding with the stored one.
The Hungarian algorithm makes the final match.
The old I D comes back only if the evidence is strong. In forensic work, a wrong identity is worse than an unresolved one.

scenes.title: Two similar people walk side by side. What risk rises?
scenes.good: That's right. Near-equal costs make the assignment easy to flip.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Near-equal costs make the assignment easy to flip.

Welcome to the case study.
Multimodal large language models can take images as well as text. They turn image patches into tokens, much like a Vision Transformer.
Could they help analyse crime-scene video the way a forensic expert would?
Research by Opeyemi Adeniran, She Model Tech, asked three questions.
How closely can multimodal models approximate human forensic reasoning?
Which prompting techniques give the most reliable, human-aligned outputs?
And how do differences between models change how well prompting works?

scenes.title: From video frames to a scored answer

beats.say: The data: five thousand seven hundred and fourteen frames from the U C F Crime video dataset, covering eleven crime categories.
Frames are loaded and encoded.
Then sent ten frames at a time to each of three models: G P T 4 o, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini two point oh Flash.
Each model replies with a structured J S O N answer.
And every answer is scored on a ten question forensic rubric, from crime type and intent, to whether the narrative is court-ready.
The study compared eight prompting strategies with the same models and frames.
Zero-shot gives a direct instruction, with no examples.
Sequential works through five stages, from a scene overview to a detailed timeline.
Least-to-most climbs eight levels, from simple objects to complex activity.
ReAct cycles through think, act, observe, and decide.
Iterative runs four rounds: people, actions, criminal elements, then a critical review.
In meta-prompting, the model writes its own specialised prompts.
Self-consistency runs five independent analyses, then takes a consensus.
And chain-of-thought takes six reasoning steps, from observation to interpretation.

scenes.title: How close to human forensic reasoning?

beats.say: Results were scored with accuracy, precision, recall and F1, plus how consistently the models agreed.
G P T 4 o came closest to human forensic reasoning, with an F1 of zero point six eight six, and accuracy zero point five eight.
Gemini came next, at zero point four five six.
Then Claude, at zero point three six five.
Across prompts, G P T 4 o stayed stable, while Claude's results varied most between techniques.
And ReAct was the most reliable technique for all three models, with consistency of one hundred, ninety point nine, and eighty one point eight percent.
beats.sql: ReAct consistency across the three models: 100% · 90.9% · 81.8%

beats.say: G P T 4 o's averaged precision was zero point six four five, and its recall zero point seven nine three.
High recall means it found most real cases.
Lower precision means about one in three of its positive calls was a false alarm: one minus zero point six four five is zero point three five five.
Plug those averages into the F1 formula, and you get zero point seven one one.
But the reported F1 is zero point six eight six. It's a macro average: F1 is computed for each of the eleven crime categories, then averaged.
beats.sql: macro F1 = average of 11 per-category F1 scores = 0.686

scenes.title: The whole course in one study

beats.say: The study pulls the course together. Images as data, from the first modules.
Deep vision models and transformers.
Evaluation metrics.
And careful reasoning about identity and events.
The take-away: how you ask matters as much as which model you use, and results must be measured, not assumed, especially when the stakes are legal.
Next for this research: more crime categories, combining prompting strategies, and making sensitive models more consistent.
